title: Negative Weights: Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall
excerpt: When an edge can be negative, Dijkstra's whole argument collapses. Bellman-Ford gives up on choosing a clever order, relaxes everything repeatedly, and detects the case where no answer exists at all.
seoTitle: Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall: Negative Weight Paths
seoDescription: Bellman-Ford explained: why negative weights break Dijkstra, why V-1 passes suffice, a full trace, how one extra pass detects negative cycles, the arbitrage application, and when the slower algorithm is the right call.

content.text: Dijkstra's algorithm rests on one assumption: adding another edge to a route can never make it cheaper. That is obviously true when every weight is a distance or a duration, and it is what lets the algorithm commit to a node's distance and never look at it again.

Some problems break the assumption. A currency exchange can leave you with more than you started. A financial model can have a step that pays out. A game can have a move that refunds. As soon as a weight can be negative, Dijkstra returns confident wrong answers, and you need something that does not rely on committing early.
Bellman-Ford's approach is almost aggressively simple: it does not try to work out a safe order to settle nodes in, and instead relaxes every edge in the graph, over and over, until nothing improves.
That sounds like it might never finish, so the question is how many passes are enough. The answer comes from thinking about what a shortest path looks like.
A shortest path never repeats a node. If it did, it would contain a loop, and removing that loop leaves a path that is no longer and visits fewer nodes. So a shortest path visits at most
V
nodes, which means it uses at most
edges.

Now watch what one full pass achieves. After the first pass, every correct distance that uses one edge is in place. After the second, every one that uses two edges is in place, because the one-edge answers it builds on were already correct. By induction, after
passes every shortest path is found, whatever order you relaxed the edges in.

That last clause is the whole tradeoff. Dijkstra needs a carefully chosen order and pays for it with a heap and a correctness proof, while Bellman-Ford needs no order at all and pays for it in time instead.
Four nodes, one negative edge, source A, and watch C get a value and then improve on it within the same pass.

body.code:
Graph: A->B 4, A->C 5, B->C -3, C->D 2

start        A 0    B inf   C inf   D inf

round 1      relax every edge once, in the order listed
  A->B       B = min(inf, 0 + 4)  = 4
  A->C       C = min(inf, 0 + 5)  = 5
  B->C       C = min(5, 4 - 3)  = 1     better route found
  C->D       D = min(inf, 1 + 2)  = 3
             A 0    B 4     C 1     D 3

round 2      relax every edge again
  nothing improves
             A 0    B 4     C 1     D 3

Nothing changed in round 2, so we can stop early.

content.text: C went to 5 via the direct edge, then dropped to 1 when the B to C edge was relaxed later in the same round. This is exactly the situation that breaks Dijkstra: it would have settled C at 5 and never revisited it, because 5 was the smallest tentative value at the time.
Also notice the early exit. The graph needed one pass, not three, and the
changed
flag caught that. The
bound is a worst case rather than a schedule, and on most real graphs the algorithm settles far sooner.

body.text: Negative cycles, and detecting them for free

content.text: There is a case where the question itself has no answer. If the graph contains a cycle whose weights sum to a negative number, you can go round it repeatedly and get cheaper every time.

body.code:
Graph: A->B 1, B->C -1, C->B -1

round 1   B = 1, C = 0
round 2   B = min(1, 0 - 1) = -1, C = -2
round 3   B = -3, C = -4
...
Every extra lap around B->C->B subtracts 2. There is no shortest path,
because "shortest" has no smallest value. Run one round past V-1 and
if anything still improves, you have found a negative cycle.

content.text: There is no shortest path here, because for any route you name there is a cheaper one, and the right response is to report that, not to return a number.
Bellman-Ford detects this almost for free. You proved above that

passes are enough for any graph where shortest paths exist. So run one extra pass. If anything still improves, no finite answer exists, and something must be looping to get cheaper. One extra loop over the edges turns the algorithm into a negative cycle detector, which is a large part of why it is still worth knowing.

That detector has real uses beyond graphs. Model currencies as nodes and exchange rates as edges, take the negative logarithm of each rate as the weight, and a negative cycle is an arbitrage opportunity: a sequence of trades returning more than you started with.

rows: Weights can be negative, or you need cycle detection

content.text: The rule is plain. Use Dijkstra whenever you can, because it is far faster. Reach for Bellman-Ford when negative weights are genuinely possible, or when detecting a negative cycle is the actual goal.
Notice the input. This one wants a flat list of edges rather than an adjacency list, since it never asks "what are this node's neighbors" and only ever sweeps every edge.
Relaxing from a node that is still unreachable.
Adding a weight to infinity gives nonsense, and in languages where infinity is a large integer it can overflow into a negative number and invent routes that do not exist. The
if (dist[from] === Infinity) continue;
line is not decoration.
Running V passes instead of V - 1, then wondering why cycle detection never fires.
The detection pass has to be the extra one, run after the bound is exhausted. Fold it in and you lose the signal.
Reporting a negative cycle that cannot reach the source.

A negative cycle in a far corner of the graph, unreachable from your start node, does not affect any distance you were asked about. If that distinction matters for your problem, check that the improving node is actually reachable.
Reaching for it by default because it is safer is a few hundred times slower on realistic inputs, and safety that costs that much is not free.
